terms.definition: A stated observation that would refute a claim, written before the run, without which surprise cannot be computed and the claim is inadmissible.

sanskrit.grammar: mf(इका)n. / m.; verbal adjective from √बाध् (bādh), 'to oppose, annul'
sanskrit.literal_gloss: setting aside, suspending, annulling; opposing, hindering
sanskrit.citation: Monier-Williams 1899, s.v. बाधक: 'setting aside, suspending, annulling, Śaṃk.; Sarvad.'; also 'opposing, hindering, injuring, prejudicing, MBh.; Pur.'

latin.grammar: noun (f., 3rd decl.) + present active participle of refūtō, agreeing in case/number
latin.literal_gloss: the refuting observation - the observation that (as it happens) refutes
latin.citation: COINED phrase. Members cited: L&S s.v. observātĭo, 'a watching, observing' (class.), 'siderum,' Cic. Div. 1, 1, 2; L&S s.v. rĕfūtātĭo, 'in rhet., a refutation,' Cic. Top. 25, 93. Derivation: observātiō (< observō, 'to watch') + present participle of refūtō ('to drive back, repel, refute'). The present participle was chosen over a future participle (refūtātūra, 'that is going to refute') deliberately, and this choice is unresolved: the concept is counterfactual ('would refute'), which Latin would more exactly carry with a subjunctive relative clause, e.g. observātiō quae refūtāret. The phrase as given may therefore be WRONG for the concept.

terms.ambiguity_notes: bādhaka carries a Nyāya/Vedānta technical freight: a bādhaka is a SUBLATING cognition, and in Advaita the sublation of the world by brahman-knowledge is the paradigm case - so the word can quietly import the doctrine that what is annulled was never real. UNI's falsifier asserts nothing of the kind: it refutes a CLAIM, not the reality of the thing claimed about. bādhaka's ordinary sense ('oppressing, harassing, paining') is unrelated and dominant outside philosophical texts. Latin refūtātiō is attested ONLY as a rhetorical operation - refuting an opponent's argument in a speech - so the Latin frames refutation as something a speaker does to an interlocutor, not something an observation does to a claim; the concept's whole force is that nobody is arguing. The counterfactual mood ('would refute') is the discriminating property and is the part every register here handles worst.

forbidden_mistranslations.why_wrong: L&S s.v. falsĭfĭcus: 'that acts falsely,' Plaut. Mil. 2, 2, 36. The word means acting deceitfully - a FORGER or a liar. A falsificator would name a person who fakes data: the precise opposite of the instrument that catches them.

terms.ambiguity_notes: EVERY register here is a FINANCIAL word. apocha, rasīd and recibo all attest specifically to money changing hands; the Latin is quoted in L&S with the rule that there is no receipt until the money is paid. UNI's receipt is an OBSERVATION that discharges a prediction, and nothing is owed or paid. The transferred property being borrowed is discharge-of-an-obligation-by-evidence, and every register imports a creditor who is not present in the concept. lekhya avoids the money but imports Dharmaśāstra litigation: MW glosses it as a written accusation or defence, i.e. a document produced in a lawsuit, which frames the receipt as adversarial. Greek ἀποχή, the etymon of apocha, independently means 'abstinence, refraining' - the Sceptical epoche - and a reader who knows Greek before Latin may read apocha as suspension of judgement, which is very nearly the opposite of closing a turn.

terms.ambiguity_notes: pramāṇa is the single most doctrinally loaded word in this file, and MW's own entry proves it: the entry cannot gloss the word without listing WHICH pramāṇas each school admits (Vedānta 6, Nyāya 4, Sāṃkhya 3). To choose pramāṇa is therefore to walk into a live school dispute about how many means of knowledge exist and what they are. UNI's A-to-U classes are NOT a pramāṇa list: they do not claim to be an exhaustive typology of valid knowing, they are not in competition with perception or inference, and they carry a ceiling ('above which no claim may ever be raised') that no pramāṇa theory has. pramāṇa also means 'authority' and 'standard' - so the rendering can be heard as saying the class MAKES the claim authoritative, when the class exists to CAP it. Latin classis imports the Servian census, where classes rank citizens by WEALTH; the rank-ordering is apt (compare CLASS_AUTHORITY_ORDERING) but the criterion - property - is not. This is a sovereign homonym with EVIDENCE (the marginal likelihood) and must never be rendered alike; it is likewise sovereign from NATURA_CLASS, which labels how a fact about NATURE is known.

terms.ambiguity_notes: The Latin is exact on the object and catastrophic on the property. L&S s.v. tabula records 'novae [tabulae], new account-books (by substituting which for the old ones debts were cancelled)' - tabulae novae was a Roman political slogan meaning DEBT ABOLITION BY REPLACING THE BOOKS. The one word Latin offers for a ledger is the word whose most famous collocation names the destruction of the record. UNI's ledger is APPEND-ONLY: substitution is the defining prohibition. A Latin reader primed on tabulae novae will hear the opposite of the concept. bahī is likewise a merchant's account-book and imports the same commercial frame; McGregor's own example (में चढ़ना, 'to enter in an account-book') is however append-shaped and mildly supports the sense. Note the corpus already uses tabulārium for the CONCLAVE append-only log; tabulae (the books) and tabulārium (the archive building) are different objects and should not be collapsed. Two sovereign ledgers exist - CLAIM-LEDGER.md and NATURE-LEDGER.md - and any register that lets one word cover both invites the merge that the file's own falsifiers forbid.

terms.ambiguity_notes: The English headword is the trap, and every register inherits it. 'Calibration' normally means ADJUSTING AN INSTRUMENT against a standard, in whichever direction the standard demands, and it is symmetric by definition. UNI's CALIBRATION is neither: it adjusts WORDING, not an instrument, and it is DOWN-ONLY. The Latin discovery here is precise and cuts against the rendering: L&S records correctio as the rhetorical figure of recalling a word to substitute 'a stronger or more significant one' - the attested Latin figure runs UPWARD, i.e. Latin's best word for this operation carries the exact license UNI forbids, which is why deorsum is not decoration but the entire fence. THE CARDINAL SIN LIVES IN THIS ENTRY: HONEST signals are NEVER calibrated. Any register that lets this word take a person's testimony as its object crosses the TRUE/HONEST sovereignty and is the worst error in the corpus. Note also that the concept requires the PRIOR wording to stay on record - a correction that quietly overwrites is not this concept, and no register above carries that requirement.

terms.ambiguity_notes: repulsa is the strongest single find in this file and also a trap. It is exactly right in structure: a repulsa is a defeat you can only suffer by STANDING FOR SOMETHING in public - you cannot be repulsed at an election you did not contest - which mirrors 'a result UNI earned' and 'missed its PRE-REGISTERED bar' with unusual precision. Horace's 'virtus, repulsae nescia sordidae' (Odes 3, 2, 17) even carries the note that the repulse is not shameful. But repulsa is a defeat inflicted BY AN ELECTORATE - someone refuses you - whereas a UNI negative is inflicted by NATURE via a bar you set yourself; and Horace's 'turpis repulsa' (Ep. 1, 1, 43) shows the word can be shameful, whereas the UNI concept is published as the credibility. terms.ambiguity_notes: The English 'baseline' is a bad word for the concept and the coinage deliberately abandons it. A baseline in ordinary scientific usage is a STARTING LEVEL measured before an intervention - a horizontal line you improve away from. M7's tuned baseline is not a starting level at all: it is a RIVAL METHOD, tuned as hard as your own, whose job is to beat you. aemulus is chosen precisely because L&S attests it as one 'striving after another earnestly ... to equal', which is the effort-symmetry the definition demands. The trap in aemulus is its bad sense: L&S records it 'in a good and bad sense' - of one who 'with a hostile feeling, strives after the possessions of another' - and 'By meton. (eccl.), an enemy'. A tuned baseline is a rival, NOT an enemy: it is built in good faith BY YOU, and the whole point is that you want it to be strong. If the rendering reads as an adversary to be defeated, the reader will do what M7 exists to stop, i.e. build a weak opponent. Note also M7's biomimetic gate rides on this concept: 'nature does it this way' earns nothing until the nature-derived design beats a tuned baseline on a pre-registered metric - so a weak rendering here weakens that gate too, and it is a NATURA-facing consequence of a UNI-side word.

terms.ambiguity_notes: Every register wants to make this a DISTINCTION, and it is an ACTION. vyāvṛtti's attested 'discrimination, distinction' senses name a difference that holds; the concept names something you DO to your own experiment to try to destroy your own result. vyāvṛtti additionally carries Buddhist apoha freight - in Dignāga's theory, vyāvṛtti/apoha is exclusion-of-the-other as the mechanism by which words refer, i.e. an entire nominalist semantics - so the word can quietly assert that meaning is constituted by exclusion. A near neighbour, viveka, is worse and must be named here: MW s.v. विवेक gives '(in Vedânta) the power of separating the invisible Spirit from the visible world (or spirit from matter, truth from untruth, reality from mere semblance or illusion)' - viveka-khyāti is the liberating discernment itself. Using viveka for a label-shuffle would dress a sanity check as soteriology. The 'load-bearing' half of the English is carried by no register: the discriminator is load-bearing because the claim RESTS on it collapsing, and a rendering that loses this leaves an ordinary robustness check.

english.definition: Removal of a mechanism in order to measure its contribution, whose number must be a computed residual and never a literal typed in by hand.

terms.ambiguity_notes: lopa is the most technically apt word in this file and the finding is worth stating plainly: Pāṇinian lopa is not a vague 'removal' but a formal DELETION OPERATION in a generative grammar, and MW's own gloss records that when lopa of an affix takes place 'a blank is substituted, which exerts the same influence on the base as the affix itself'. That is a startlingly exact parallel to an ablation done wrong - the Pāṇinian blank STILL ACTS, i.e. deleting the element does not remove its effect - and any UNI ablation in which the removed mechanism's influence persists through a substituted blank is precisely the leakage the concept exists to detect. This should be read as a caution the grammarians already recorded, NOT as a nature citation and NOT as raising any UNI rung. lopa's ordinary senses ('breaking, hurting, injury, destruction'; 'neglect, violation, transgression of a vow') are unrelated and dominant outside grammar. The Latin ablatio is attested but only ecclesiastically and only in the bare sense 'a taking away': it does not carry 'in order to measure its contribution', which is the whole purpose clause. NO REGISTER carries the computed-residual requirement, which is the concept's actual fence: an ablation number typed by hand is a claim about a run that did not happen.

terms.ambiguity_notes: Two independent finds converge here and both should be recorded. (1) MW s.v. नियम (niyama) gives '(in Mīmāṃsā phil.) a rule or precept (laying down or specifying something otherwise optional)' - which is a startlingly exact description of pre-registration's mechanism: it BINDS IN ADVANCE what would otherwise be a free, data-contingent choice, and freedom of analytic choice is precisely what the definition names as the inflation source. niyama is not used as the headword only because MW also anchors it to the Yoga limbs and to 'penance, piety', which would import an ascetic frame. (2) pratijñā is chosen because in Nyāya it is the FIRST member of the syllogism, stated before the reason and the example, and it BINDS the debater: abandoning one's pratijñā (pratijñā-hāni) is itself a recognised point of defeat. Classical Indian dialectics thus already penalised the failure mode the definition describes. This is a note about a shared structure, NOT a nature citation and NOT a UNI gate. The freight to watch: pratijñā's dominant ordinary sense is a solemn VOW, which moralises the act - pre-registration is not a promise to be virtuous, and the definition is explicit that the problem arises 'with no deliberate p-hacking at all', i.e. it is not about honesty. Latin professio has the same defect from the other side: it is also 'a business or profession which one publicly avows', so it can read as a vocation.

forbidden_mistranslations.rendering: any rendering as a vow or oath (Sk. व्रत vrata, Sp. juramento, Hi. शपथ)
forbidden_mistranslations.why_wrong: Moralises the concept. Pre-registration is not a pledge of good behaviour; the definition explicitly locates the harm in REASONABLE choices made with no deliberate p-hacking. A vow implies the danger is bad faith, which is the wrong diagnosis and licenses 'I am honest, so I need not pre-register'.

forbidden_mistranslations.rendering: Latin professio alone

forbidden_mistranslations.rendering: any rendering as 'hypothesis' or 'the claim to be proved' alone
forbidden_mistranslations.why_wrong: pratijñā's logical sense is the proposition to be proved. Pre-registration fixes the BAR, the MARGIN, the THRESHOLD, the named ABLATION and the STOPPING RULE - the decision procedure, not the claim. A rendering that names only the thesis loses the stopping rule, which is where the inflation actually enters.

forbidden_mistranslations.why_wrong: RAE s.v. registro: 'Acción de registrar'; it also strongly carries 'search'. Reads as administrative enrolment, and drops 'before the build' entirely.

latin.citation: COINED phrase. Member cited: L&S s.v. ob-signo: 'to seal, seal up a will, a letter, etc. (class.) ... Esp.: tabulas, testamenta, to sign and seal, as a witness ... Prov.: agere cum aliquo tabellis obsignatis, to deal with one with sealed writings, i. e. in the strictest form, Cic. Tusc. 5, 11, 33 ... tabulas obsignare velle, would seal up the documents, i. e. would have no discussion, Cic. Pis. 28, 69'. 'pars' was NOT fetched from L&S in this pass. terms.ambiguity_notes: The Latin idiom is unusually well-suited and the reason is worth recording: L&S s.v. obsigno preserves Cicero's 'tabulas obsignare velle', glossed 'would seal up the documents, i.e. WOULD HAVE NO DISCUSSION' (Pis. 28, 69), and 'agere cum aliquo tabellis obsignatis ... in the strictest form' (Tusc. 5, 11, 33). Roman sealing was therefore already a device meaning THIS IS CLOSED TO FURTHER ARGUMENT, which is exactly the force of seal-before-scoring - the seal is not about secrecy, it is about foreclosing renegotiation. The gap: obsignāta carries the seal but NOT the once-only sentinel, and 'touched exactly ONCE' is the discriminating property. A Roman seal could be broken and the tablets re-sealed; the concept forbids the second touch outright. Also note that the Latin's native object is tabulae (documents), which collides with LEDGER's rendering - a reviewer must ensure the two do not converge on the same phrase. The word 'held' in English is a trap in its own right: the corpus bans 'held-PASS' in author voice, and the set is not 'held' in the sense of being possessed but in the sense of being WITHHELD.

forbidden_mistranslations.rendering: any rendering as 'secret' or 'hidden' (Lat. arcānus, Sp. datos secretos)
forbidden_mistranslations.why_wrong: The seal is not about concealment - the data may be perfectly well known. It is about foreclosing a second scoring. Secrecy is the wrong mechanism and would license 'nobody looked, so it is fine'.

forbidden_mistranslations.rendering: any rendering as 'reserved' or 'set aside' that drops the once-only sentinel (Sp. conjunto reservado)
forbidden_mistranslations.why_wrong: Reserving data says nothing about how many times it may be scored. The definition's whole force is 'touched exactly ONCE' - a set scored twice is a training set with a good reputation.

forbidden_mistranslations.rendering: any rendering importing 'held-PASS'
forbidden_mistranslations.why_wrong: 'held-PASS' is banned in author voice by the honesty rail. The set being held says nothing about the outcome.

back_translation_test.test: Give a translator the rendering and ask: how many times may this data be scored, and what happens if it is scored a second time?
back_translation_test.pass_criterion: PASS only if the answer is EXACTLY ONCE and that a second scoring converts it into a training set. Any answer about secrecy, or permitting a re-score after re-sealing, FAILS.

terms.confidence: LOW. Only Latin attempted, as a coinage with one member uncited; the once-only sentinel - the actual discriminating property - is carried by nothing. Three registers honestly not attempted rather than invented.

hindi.citation: McGregor, Oxford Hindi-English Dictionary, p. 1021, s.v. सीमा sīmā [S.], f. '1. limit, boundary; frontier. 2. bounds, limit (of morality or convention).' NOTE: this cites the general-language word for a boundary ONLY; it does NOT attest a confidence-interval bound, and the statistical sense is unsupported here.

Arma defensiva del cuerpo usada antiguamente ...' - the chain-mail sense - and the meta description truncates before any mathematical sense. The mathematical sense is therefore NOT CONFIRMED and 'cota' is not proposed on this evidence.

terms.ambiguity_notes: This is a RULE about which number to quote, and no register above renders the rule - each renders only the word 'bound', which is the easy half. The load-bearing content is the CONTRAST ('never the point estimate') and the RELATION ('the bound that excludes the threshold' - a specific one of the two bounds, selected by which side the threshold falls on). A one-word rendering therefore cannot carry the concept and must not be treated as if it does. The 1919 eclipse is the worked case recorded in the concept's own notes: the result severely EXCLUDED the Newtonian value and was consistent with but did not pin the GR value; the excluding bound is the verdict and the point estimate is decoration. Latin terminus imports a god - L&S records Terminus as 'the deity presiding over boundaries' - and Roman boundary stones were sacred and IMMOVABLE, which is a poor frame for a bound that shifts with the data. avadhi and sīmā are both ordinary spatial/temporal boundary words with no statistical content whatever; sīmā's second McGregor sense is 'bounds, limit (of morality or convention)', i.e. propriety.

forbidden_mistranslations.rendering: any rendering that names the interval rather than the bound (Sp. intervalo de confianza, Hi. विश्वास अंतराल)
forbidden_mistranslations.why_wrong: The verdict is ONE bound - the one excluding the threshold - not the interval and not both ends. Naming the interval restores the ambiguity M2 exists to remove.

forbidden_mistranslations.rendering: any rendering as 'estimate', 'value' or 'result' (Sk. मान māna, Sp. estimación)
forbidden_mistranslations.why_wrong: The point estimate is exactly what the rule forbids quoting as the verdict. Rendering the concept with an estimate word inverts it.

forbidden_mistranslations.rendering: Latin terminus read through the god / the sacred boundary stone
forbidden_mistranslations.why_wrong: A Roman terminus was sacred and immovable. A confidence bound is neither, and moves with the evidence.

forbidden_mistranslations.rendering: Hindi सीमा sīmā in its moral sense
forbidden_mistranslations.why_wrong: McGregor's sense 2 is 'bounds, limit (of morality or convention)'. Reads as propriety, not as a statistical bound.

back_translation_test.test: Give a translator the rendering plus a result (point estimate 1.7, CI [1.2, 2.2], threshold 0.9) and ask what the verdict is.
back_translation_test.pass_criterion: PASS only if the answer names 1.2 - the bound excluding the threshold - and explicitly declines to report 1.7 as the verdict. Any answer quoting the point estimate or the whole interval FAILS. Every register above is expected to FAIL this, since none renders the rule.

terms.confidence: LOW. The attestations are genuine but they attest ordinary boundary words; the concept is a verdict RULE and is not rendered by any of them. Recorded as a known structural gap, not as a near miss.

terms.definition: Mayo's requirement that a passing test counts as evidence only if it could have failed, made operable as the single question: if the claim were false, what is the probability this exact procedure would still have passed it?

english.definition: Mayo's requirement that a passing test counts as evidence only if it could have failed, made operable as the single question: if the claim were false, what is the probability this exact procedure would still have passed it?

Riguroso, áspero, duro en el trato o el castigo. 2. adj. Exacto y rígido en la observancia de una ley, un precepto o una regla.' - harshness in treatment or punishment. See forbidden_mistranslations. No replacement confirmed in this pass.

terms.ambiguity_notes: THE CENTRAL ERROR THIS ENTRY EXISTS TO PREVENT: severity is a property OF A TEST PROCEDURE, and every register renders it as a property OF A PERSON'S CHARACTER. L&S s.v. severitas is a moral word throughout - the sternness of censors, 'tristis severitas inest in vultu', severity opposed to lepos, to comitas, to mansuetudo - and RAE s.v. severo confirms the same in Spanish ('duro en el trato o el castigo'). Mayo's severity has nothing to do with sternness: a severe test is one that WOULD PROBABLY HAVE FAILED had the claim been false, and a stern examiner running a test that cannot fail achieves severity ZERO. The two notions are not merely different, they are uncorrelated, and the natural-language word actively teaches the wrong one. parīkṣā and Hindi parīkṣā name the test itself, not the property of it, and both carry 'trial by ordeal' - MW cross-references दिव्य - which is a test whose outcome is determined by divine intervention rather than by the claim's truth: the limiting case of a test with no severity at all. As the concept's own note records, a weak pass and a severe pass are different species of result and must never share a column.

forbidden_mistranslations.rendering: Latin saevitia
forbidden_mistranslations.why_wrong: L&S s.v. saevĭtĭa: 'a raging, rage, fierceness, ferocity ... harshness, savageness, cruelty, barbarity, severity'. It glosses AS 'severity' in English while meaning savagery, and it is a near-homophone of severitas. The single most available wrong word here.

forbidden_mistranslations.rendering: Spanish severidad
forbidden_mistranslations.why_wrong: RAE: 'Cualidad de severo'; severo = 'Riguroso, áspero, duro en el trato o el castigo'. Says harshness of treatment or punishment. A severe test in Mayo's sense is not harsh and need not be strict; it merely could have failed.

forbidden_mistranslations.rendering: any rendering as strictness or rigour of the examiner (Sk. कठोरता kaṭhoratā, Hi. कठोरता)
forbidden_mistranslations.why_wrong: Relocates the property from the procedure to the person. A stern examiner administering a test that cannot fail has severity zero; a mild one administering a test that would have caught the error has high severity.

forbidden_mistranslations.rendering: any rendering via 'trial by ordeal' (Sk. दिव्य divya)
forbidden_mistranslations.why_wrong: An ordeal's outcome is decided by divine intervention, not by whether the claim is false. It is the exact zero-severity case: the probability of passing is independent of the truth of the claim.

forbidden_mistranslations.rendering: any rendering as 'difficulty' (Sp. dificultad, Hi. कठिनता)
forbidden_mistranslations.why_wrong: A difficult test can still be one the claim would pass whether or not it were true. Severity is about the counterfactual failure probability, not about how hard the test is.

back_translation_test.test: Give a translator the rendering and ask: (a) is this a property of the test or of the person running it, and (b) if the claim were false, what would this quantity tell you?
back_translation_test.pass_criterion: PASS only if (a) OF THE TEST and (b) the probability the procedure would still have passed it. Any answer naming a person's disposition, harshness, or difficulty FAILS. severitas and severidad are expected to FAIL.

terms.confidence: HIGH on the attestations and HIGH on the diagnosis that all of them are wrong for the concept. This entry's value is its forbidden list, not its renderings: Latin and Spanish are confirmed traps and parīkṣā names the test rather than the property. A coinage is likely required.

terms.definition: Platt's procedure of devising alternative hypotheses, devising a crucial experiment each of whose possible outcomes EXCLUDES one or more of them, carrying it out to a clean result, and recycling.

english.definition: Platt's procedure of devising alternative hypotheses, devising a crucial experiment each of whose possible outcomes EXCLUDES one or more of them, carrying it out to a clean result, and recycling.

hindi.citation: McGregor, Oxford Hindi-English Dictionary, p. 37, s.v. अनुमान anu-mān [S.], m. '1. inference. 2. notion; opinion. 3. conjecture; estimate; guess.'

terms.ambiguity_notes: 'Strong' is the trap and it is a trap in English first. Platt's inference is not strong in the sense of forceful, confident or well-supported; it is strong because each experiment's every outcome KILLS at least one hypothesis. The strength is a property of the experimental DESIGN's exclusion structure, not of the conclusion's confidence. Any register that renders 'strong' with a vigour word (Lat. fortis, validus; Sp. fuerte; Hi. मज़बूत) says 'a confident inference', which is close to the opposite - a confident inference with no exclusion structure is exactly the storytelling Platt attacks. This is why the Latin coinage renders the MECHANISM (excludēns) and drops the adjective. anumān/anumāna are the standard words for inference in both Sanskrit and Hindi, but they carry Nyāya freight: anumāna is one of the pramāṇas, operating via vyāpti (invariable concomitance) and a hetu - a positive machinery for establishing a conclusion, whereas Platt's procedure is eliminative and its output is a hypothesis DESTROYED. As the concept's own note records: an experiment whose every outcome leaves all hypotheses alive is not an experiment, it is an expense; and if the outcome-to-exclusion mapping was not written before the run, you did storytelling with a dataset - which ties this concept to PRE_REGISTRATION and should not be rendered as if it were free-standing.

forbidden_mistranslations.rendering: any rendering of 'strong' as forceful or robust (Lat. fortis / validus, Sp. fuerte, Hi. मज़बूत)
forbidden_mistranslations.why_wrong: Says the inference is confident or well-supported. Platt's strength is the exclusion structure of the design. A confident inference with no exclusions is the very thing the procedure is aimed against.

forbidden_mistranslations.rendering: Latin illātiō alone
forbidden_mistranslations.why_wrong: L&S: 'a carrying or bringing in (post-class.)'; its literal senses include 'mortui', i.e. burial, and 'an impost, duty'. Unfenced it reads as interment or a tax; and it names inference in general, losing the exclusion requirement entirely.

forbidden_mistranslations.rendering: Sanskrit अनुमान anumāna used bare
forbidden_mistranslations.why_wrong: Names inference as such - a pramāṇa that ESTABLISHES conclusions via vyāpti. Platt's procedure ELIMINATES alternatives. Bare anumāna loses both the plurality of hypotheses and the exclusion.

forbidden_mistranslations.rendering: any rendering as 'deduction' or 'logical reasoning' in general

terms.ambiguity_notes: Chamberlin's remedy is PLURALITY, NOT NEUTRALITY, and the distinction is what every rendering is likely to lose. The method does not ask you to suspend judgement or hold no view; it asks you to hold SEVERAL LIVE VIEWS AT ONCE, each of which you actually work. Any register that drifts toward 'open-mindedness', 'impartiality' or 'suspension of judgement' has rendered neutrality and missed the concept - and Latin makes this drift easy, since the obvious neighbouring vocabulary (dubitātiō, suspēnsiō) is Sceptical. Two further properties are load-bearing and unrendered: 'at least two always, at least three to claim' (a COUNT), and 'structurally distinct in mechanism rather than in parameter' (a DISTINCTNESS CRITERION - two settings of one model are ONE hypothesis, not two). The named failure mode is parental affection for one's own explanation; the payoff is that disputes become conflicts between ideas rather than between people. Note also the concept's own warning: one hypothesis plus a null is NOT this, since the null is usually a strawman you already know how to beat - so a rendering that permits 'my idea vs. nothing' satisfies the words and defeats the concept. 'Working' in English means actively worked, not provisional; conjectūra is chosen with reservation because L&S's own gloss ('a guess') undersells a hypothesis one is committed to testing.

The faction sense is actively harmful here: it makes rival hypotheses into rival PARTIES, restoring the person-vs-person conflict the method exists to convert into idea-vs-idea.

forbidden_mistranslations.rendering: any rendering of 'working' as provisional, tentative or draft
forbidden_mistranslations.why_wrong: A working hypothesis is one you actively WORK, not one you hold loosely. Tentativeness is neutrality wearing a different coat.

terms.ambiguity_notes: The discriminating property is BY ANOTHER PARTY, and it is the property every register drops. āvṛtti, repetītiō and every 'repetition' word describe doing the same thing again - which the ORIGINAL author can do, and which is not replication at all but merely a repeated run. The concept's entire function is to separate OBSERVED-REPLICATED from OBSERVED-SINGLE, and that boundary is drawn by WHO did it, not by how many times it was done. Hence aliēnus is not a modifier but the load-bearing word; its own trap is that aliēnus also means 'estranged, hostile, unfavourable, averse', so 'repetitio aliena' can read as a hostile repetition, when the replicator's disposition is irrelevant. āvṛtti carries a heavy doctrinal sense MW records directly: 'worldly existence, the revolution of births, Kap.' - āvṛtti is the turning of saṃsāra, so the word can import rebirth. The concept's note is load-bearing and unrendered anywhere: 'Nobody has tried' is a fact about the literature and is printed as one; a single unreplicated measurement can never move a UNI rung - least of all via OBSERVED-SINGLE, the class that exists precisely to stop one study being read as settled.

terms.ambiguity_notes: The concept's fence is the SURVIVAL CLAUSE - 'survives the hunt for instrument error' - and not one register carries it. Every word above names an irregularity as such; UNI's anomaly is an irregularity that has ALREADY been hunted and has not died, which is a completely different epistemic object, and calling an unexamined residual an anomaly is the characteristic abuse. The instrument's own error is the FIRST term to hunt, not the last to add: OPERA's 60.7 ns was a loose fibre connector, and publishing the anomaly with its error budget and then its own refutation was the method working, not failing. Also unrendered: 'quantitatively characterized' - as the concept's note records, an anomaly you cannot describe quantitatively is a rumour. The register-specific freight is heavy. Latin anomalia is attested ONLY inside the ancient grammarians' analogia/anomalia controversy, i.e. the dispute over whether language is regular by rule or by usage - so the Latin word is a partisan term in a linguistic quarrel, not a word for an empirical residual. RAE's third sense makes anomalía an ANGLE in orbital mechanics (a purely technical, non-pejorative coordinate), so a Spanish reader in a physics register may hear a parameter. vyabhicāra's dominant non-technical sense is devastating: MW gives 'trespass, transgression, crime, vice, sin (esp. infidelity of a wife)'.

forbidden_mistranslations.why_wrong: Exactly inverts the concept. An anomaly is what remains AFTER error and defect have been hunted and excluded. Calling it a defect assigns it to the instrument - the hypothesis the survival clause has already had to defeat.

english.definition: A run proving the instrument can detect the effect it is looking for, without which a negative result is a hypothesis rather than a finding.

terms.ambiguity_notes: 'Control' is the problem: no register has an attested word for the experimental sense, and every available word means GOVERNANCE, RESTRAINT or SUPERVISION. A positive control does not control anything - it is a run whose answer is already known, used to check that the instrument can speak. The Latin coinage therefore drops 'control' entirely and renders the FUNCTION. The most valuable note here is doctrinal and runs the opposite way from the usual freight: MW s.v. अन्-उपलब्धि (anupalabdhi) gives 'non-perception, non-recognition', and anupalabdhi is admitted in Mīmāṃsā and Advaita as a PRAMĀṆA - a valid means of knowing ABSENCE, i.e. the doctrine that not perceiving X can establish that X is not there. That is precisely the inference the positive control exists to BLOCK. The two must never be rendered with one word or read as allies: where anupalabdhi licenses inferring absence from non-perception, the positive-control rule says non-perception establishes NOTHING until the instrument has been shown able to perceive. Recording this as a structural opposition between the concept and a classical doctrine; it is NOT a nature citation and raises no UNI rung. NA-03 names it 'the positive control nobody runs'. This program learned it the hard way: ICMP silence was read as a dead fleet; the fleet was fine and the firewall drops ICMP. The same error class was live during the authoring of this very file - blank API responses were nearly read as 'not in Monier-Williams' until a query for deva confirmed the instrument worked.

forbidden_mistranslations.why_wrong: Says the instrument is being governed or restrained. A positive control governs nothing; it demonstrates detection capability. MW s.v. नियम gives 'restraining, checking, holding back, preventing, controlling' - exactly the wrong sense, and niyama is in any case needed near PRE_REGISTRATION.

forbidden_mistranslations.why_wrong: MW: 'non-perception, non-recognition'. It names the doctrine that absence can be KNOWN by non-perception - the inference the positive control exists to forbid. Rendering the guard with the name of the error it guards against is the worst available inversion in this entry.

forbidden_mistranslations.why_wrong: A control group is a comparison arm within an experiment. A positive control is a run with a KNOWN answer used to validate the instrument itself. It also collides with BASELINE, a separate concept in this file.

forbidden_mistranslations.why_wrong: Without the positive control a negative result is a HYPOTHESIS, not a finding. That downgrade is the concept's entire output and must survive translation.

terms.ambiguity_notes: Every register names the ORIGIN; the concept is the RECORD OF the origin, kept to an operational standard. The difference is the whole concept: an origin is a fact about the past, while provenance is a maintained artefact whose adequacy has a test - 'kept well enough that the loose connector can be found'. mūla, origo and procedencia all name where a thing came from and none names the keeping of it, which is why the Latin leads with index (the register) rather than with origo. A genuine convergence is worth recording: MW glosses मूल as 'an original text (as opp. to the commentary or gloss)', and McGregor gives मूल-ग्रंथ 'original text (of a work)' - the mūla/commentary distinction is exactly the separation SIGNUM SIGNUM MANET requires, where the signal and the commentary about it travel separately and an attribution is never merged. This is a structural parallel in the lexicon, NOT a UNI gate and NOT a nature claim. The reason OPERA could kill its own claim was provenance of this kind. Distinct from the provenance FENCE classes (NOT-SOURCED / NOT-CONFIRMED / NOT-LOCATED), which record gaps in this corpus's own homework and must not be rendered with the same word. index carries a serious trap of its own: L&S records it 'Esp., in a bad sense, an informer, betrayer, spy'.

latin.grammar: rēgula (ae, f.) + cavum (i, n.) in the genitive
latin.citation: COINED phrase; both members CITED. L&S s.v. rēgŭla: 'ae, f. rego, a straight piece of wood, ruler, rule (class.; cf.: norma, libella)'; 'II. Trop., a rule, pattern, model, example'. L&S s.v. căvus: 'a, um, adj., hollow, excavated, concave (opp. plenus, full ...)'; 'B. Subst.: căvum, i, n. ... a hollow, cavity, hole, Cato, R. R. 128; Plaut. Men. 1, 2, 49; Lucr. 5, 1382; Liv. 24, 34, 9'. Derivation: regula + cavum in the genitive. NOTE: this is a CALQUE OF A CALQUE - 'cavity' is already a metaphor imported from the physics cavity method, and rendering the metaphor's vehicle into Latin transmits the picture while transmitting none of the mathematics.

english.definition: M22's rule that a hierarchy level must never treat an upstream prior as fresh evidence, but must divide it out.

terms.ambiguity_notes: The concept's own note is explicit and binding: 'Cavity' is a term of art borrowed from cavity methods, NOT an anatomical or dental sense. This makes the concept nearly untranslatable by word, because the English name is a metaphor whose vehicle ('a hollow') carries none of the content: the content is that a level must DIVIDE OUT the upstream prior rather than count it again, and 'cavity' names the leave-one-out hole in the physics method from which the technique takes its name. Any register that translates the vehicle produces a word about holes and communicates nothing - the Latin above does exactly this and is offered with that defect stated, not concealed. A translator who does not know the cavity method will produce an anatomical word in every language. The honest options are (a) leave the term untranslated and gloss the rule, or (b) name the RULE rather than the metaphor - something on the order of 'the rule against counting one's own prior twice' - which no register above attempts. Double-counting your own prior is how a hierarchy manufactures confidence from nothing, and that sentence, not the word 'cavity', is what must survive.

forbidden_mistranslations.rendering: any anatomical or dental rendering (Sp. cavidad, Hi. गुहा/कोटर, Lat. caverna)
forbidden_mistranslations.why_wrong: The concept's own note forbids it explicitly: cavity here is a term of art from cavity methods, not an anatomical or dental sense. A dental caries word is pure noise.

forbidden_mistranslations.rendering: any rendering as 'emptiness' or 'void' (Sk. शून्य śūnya, Lat. inane)
forbidden_mistranslations.why_wrong: śūnya imports Madhyamaka emptiness - an entire Buddhist metaphysics - onto a bookkeeping rule about not double-counting a prior. The most extravagant possible category error in this file.

forbidden_mistranslations.rendering: any rendering that keeps the metaphor's vehicle without the rule
forbidden_mistranslations.why_wrong: 'Cavity' communicates nothing on its own. The translatable object is 'divide out the upstream prior; never treat it as fresh evidence'. A faithful rendering of the hole is an unfaithful rendering of the concept.

back_translation_test.test: Give a translator the rendering and ask: what must a level of the hierarchy do with information it received from upstream, and what goes wrong if it does not?
back_translation_test.pass_criterion: PASS only if the answer is DIVIDE IT OUT / do not count it as fresh evidence, and that otherwise the hierarchy manufactures confidence from nothing. Any answer mentioning holes, teeth or emptiness FAILS. rēgula cavī is expected to FAIL and is retained only as a placeholder with its defect recorded.

terms.confidence: LOW, and deliberately so. This is the least translatable concept in the file: its English name is a metaphor borrowed from statistical physics, and every register that renders the metaphor renders nothing. The recommendation on the evidence is to leave it untranslated and gloss the rule.
